cards.front: Name the five labeled regions of the periodic table.
cards.back: Alkali metals, Alkaline earth metals, Transition metals, Halogens, Noble gases

cards.front: Match each group number with its family name.
cards.back: Group 1 = alkali metals, 2 = alkaline earth, 17 = halogens, 18 = noble gases.

cards.front: How many valence electrons does a main-group element have?
cards.back: Group 1: 1. Group 2: 2. Groups 13-18: group number minus 10 (halogens 7, noble gases 8; helium has 2).

cards.front: Why are the noble gases so unreactive?
cards.back: Their outer shell is full (an octet; helium has a full 1s²), so they neither gain nor lose electrons easily.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a neon atom and a sodium atom as rings with dots. Circle the full outer ring of neon and the lonely outer dot of sodium.

cards.front: Transition metals fill {{d}} orbitals, often form ions with {{more than one}} charge (Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺) and many make {{colored}} compounds.
cards.back: d-block elements sit in Groups 3-12.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a row of five test tubes with colored solutions (Cu²⁺ blue, Fe³⁺ yellow-brown, MnO₄⁻ purple) and label the ions.

cards.front: Put the alkali metals in order of INCREASING reactivity with water.
cards.back: Li → Na → K → Rb → Cs (reactivity grows down the group).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a column of five beakers. Add bigger splashes and flames going down, and an arrow labeled 'more reactive'.

cards.front: Which three materials stop alpha, beta and gamma radiation? (named in the diagram)
cards.back: Paper, Aluminum, Lead

cards.front: Alpha decay: the nucleus loses {{2}} protons and {{2}} neutrons, so the mass number drops by {{4}}.
cards.back: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, ⁴₂He.

cards.front: What happens to Z and A in beta-minus decay?
cards.back: A neutron turns into a proton and an electron (the beta particle). Z goes up by 1; the mass number A stays the same.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a nucleus with a grey neutron turning gold (proton) and an electron flying out. Write 'Z → Z + 1, A unchanged'.

cards.front: Half-life: N = N₀ × ({{½}})^{{n}} where n = time ÷ half-life.
cards.back: After 3 half-lives only 1/8 is left.

cards.front: Match each particle with its symbol.
cards.back: alpha = ⁴₂He, beta-minus = ⁰₋₁e, gamma = γ, neutron = ¹₀n.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four small boxes, one per particle, each with the symbol and its charge written under it.

cards.front: How do you calculate the relative atomic mass of an element with isotopes?
cards.back: A weighted average: add (fractional abundance × isotope mass) for each isotope. Example: 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37 gives 35.5.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a bar chart: a tall bar at 35 (75%) and a short bar at 37 (25%). Mark the average 35.5 closer to the tall bar.

cards.front: Name the labeled orbitals in the energy ladder.
Put the orbitals in the order they fill (lowest energy first).
How many electrons fit in an s, p and d subshell? And in shell n?
cards.back: s: 2, p: 6, d: 10. Shell n holds 2n² electrons (n = 3 holds 18).

cards.front: State the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule.
cards.back: Pauli: an orbital holds at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins. Hund: fill each orbital of a subshell with one electron (same spin) before pairing up.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three p boxes. Fill them ↑ ↑ ↑ for N, then ↑↓ ↑ ↑ for O. Cross out a version that pairs early.

cards.front: Quantum numbers: l = 0 is {{s}}, l = 1 is {{p}}, l = 2 is {{d}}; mₗ runs from {{-l}} to {{+l}}.
cards.back: n is the shell; l gives the shape; mₗ the orientation.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw an s sphere, a p dumbbell along x, y and z, and write l = 0 and l = 1 under them.

cards.front: What is the ground-state configuration of Cr and of Cu?
cards.back: Cr: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵. Cu: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰. A half-full or full d subshell is extra stable.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the 4s and five 3d boxes for Cr with six single arrows, and for Cu with 4s single and 3d all paired.

cards.front: What is the difference between paramagnetic and diamagnetic?
cards.back: Paramagnetic: at least one unpaired electron, pulled into a magnetic field (Fe has 4 unpaired). Diamagnetic: all paired, weakly repelled (Zn).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a magnet with an iron atom (4 single arrows) pulled in and a zinc atom (all paired arrows) pushed away.

cards.front: Which three trends are written in the box?
cards.back: Ionization energy, Electronegativity, Atomic radius

cards.front: How does atomic radius change across a period and down a group?
cards.back: Across a period it decreases (more protons pull the same shell closer). Down a group it increases (extra shells).

cards.front: Which element has the highest electronegativity, and which the lowest?
cards.back: Fluorine is highest (4.0 on the Pauling scale). Cesium and francium are the lowest.

cards.front: Why is the first ionization energy of oxygen lower than nitrogen's?
cards.back: In O, one 2p orbital holds a PAIR of electrons that repel each other, so one is easier to remove. Similar dip: Be to B.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw ionization energy against atomic number for Li to Ne as a zigzag. Mark the two dips at B and O.

cards.front: Put in order of INCREASING atomic radius.
cards.back: F → O → N → C → Li
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw six circles of growing size labeled F, O, N, C, Li from left to right.

cards.front: How do cation and anion sizes compare with their atoms? What about isoelectronic ions?
cards.back: Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger. For isoelectronic ions, more protons means smaller: Al³⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw Na and Na⁺ side by side (Na⁺ clearly smaller), then Cl and Cl⁻ (Cl⁻ clearly larger).

cards.front: Which halogen releases the most energy when it gains an electron (most negative electron affinity)?
cards.back: Chlorine, not fluorine. Fluorine is so small that the extra electron is crowded by its dense 2p electrons.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw F and Cl as circles (F smaller). Show an electron arriving at each and write 'crowded' next to F.

cards.front: Name the three bond types in the picture.
cards.back: Ionic, Covalent, Metallic

cards.front: Name the three VSEPR geometries in the picture.
cards.back: Linear, Trigonal planar, Tetrahedral

cards.front: Match each molecular shape with its ideal bond angle.
cards.back: Linear 180°, trigonal planar 120°, tetrahedral 109.5°, bent (H₂O) 104.5°, pyramidal (NH₃) 107°.

cards.front: Which hybridization goes with 2, 3 and 4 electron regions?
cards.back: 2 regions: sp (linear: CO₂, C₂H₂). 3 regions: sp² (trigonal planar: BF₃, C₂H₄). 4 regions: sp³ (tetrahedral: CH₄, NH₃, H₂O).

cards.front: Order these attractions from WEAKEST to STRONGEST (typical).
cards.back: London dispersion → dipole-dipole → hydrogen bond → ionic bond
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four arrows of growing thickness, each labeled with one attraction.

cards.front: When can molecules form hydrogen bonds?
cards.back: When H is bonded to N, O or F, and a neighboring molecule has a lone pair on N, O or F. Examples: H₂O, NH₃, HF.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two water molecules. Draw a dotted line from an H of one to the O of the other and label it 'hydrogen bond'.

cards.front: What kind of oxides are acidic, basic and amphoteric?
cards.back: Metal oxides are basic (Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH). Nonmetal oxides are acidic (CO₂, SO₃). Al₂O₃ and ZnO are amphoteric (react with both).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a line from left to right across period 3 (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃) shading basic → amphoteric → acidic.

cards.front: Name the five reaction types.
cards.back: Synthesis, Decomposition, Single replacement, Double replacement, Combustion

cards.front: Name the four boxes of the mole map.
cards.back: Mass, Moles, Particles, Gas volume

cards.front: n = m ÷ {{M}}; particles N = n × {{6.02 × 10²³}}; gas volume at STP V = n × {{22.4 L}}.
cards.back: M is molar mass in g/mol. At STP (0 °C, 1 atm) 1 mol of gas is 22.4 L.

cards.front: Empirical formula: grams → {{moles}} → divide by the {{smallest}} → multiply to get {{whole numbers}}.
cards.back: Example: C 40%, H 6.7%, O 53.3% gives C:H:O = 1:2:1, so CH₂O.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four boxes in a row for the four steps, with the C/H/O example filled in under them.

cards.front: Balance: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
cards.back: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Balance C first, then H, and O last.
cards.sketch_prompt: Write the equation and make a small table of atoms left/right (C, H, O). Fix one row at a time.

cards.front: How do you find the limiting reactant?
cards.back: Convert each amount to moles and divide by its coefficient. The smallest result is the limiting reactant; it decides how much product forms.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw sandwiches: 2 slices of bread per 1 slice of cheese. Count how many sandwiches 10 bread and 3 cheese can make.

cards.front: Match each reaction with its type.
cards.back: Synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement.

cards.front: Name the two labeled parts of the beaker.
cards.back: Solute, Solution volume

cards.front: Molarity M = {{moles of solute}} ÷ {{liters of solution}}; molality m = moles of solute ÷ {{kg of solvent}}.
cards.back: Molarity uses the whole solution; molality uses only the solvent.

cards.front: Dilution: {{M₁V₁}} = {{M₂V₂}}, because the moles of solute stay the same.
cards.back: Add solvent only; the amount of solute does not change.

cards.front: Water self-ionization: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = {{1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴}} at 25 °C, so pH + pOH = {{14}}.
cards.back: Pure water: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = 7.

cards.front: Name the three zones of the pH scale.
cards.back: Acidic, Neutral, Basic

cards.front: Which salts make acidic, basic or neutral solutions?
cards.back: Strong acid + strong base (NaCl): neutral. Weak acid + strong base (sodium acetate): basic. Strong acid + weak base (NH₄Cl): acidic.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a 2 × 2 table: acid strong/weak across, base strong/weak down. Fill each box with an example salt and write acidic, basic or neutral.

cards.front: Does pure water at 50 °C have pH 7?
cards.back: No. Kw rises with temperature (5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 50 °C) so pH ≈ 6.63. It is still NEUTRAL because [H⁺] = [OH⁻].
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the pH scale with a tick at 7 (25 °C) and another at 6.63 (50 °C) both labeled 'neutral'.

cards.front: Name the four boxes of the conjugate-pair picture.
cards.back: Acid, Base, Conjugate base, Conjugate acid

cards.front: State the Arrhenius, Brønsted and Lewis definitions of an acid.
cards.back: Arrhenius: gives H⁺ in water. Brønsted: donates H⁺. Lewis: accepts an electron pair (so BF₃ is a Lewis acid).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three small panels: H⁺ leaving HCl in water; H⁺ jumping from one molecule to another; an arrow of electrons from NH₃ to BF₃.

cards.back: Each pH step is a factor of 10 in [H⁺].

cards.front: For a weak acid, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [{{HA}}]. For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = {{Kw}}.
cards.back: A bigger Ka means a stronger acid.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw HA splitting into H⁺ and A⁻ with a double arrow; write Ka under the arrow.

cards.front: Write the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation and when a buffer works best.
cards.back: pH = pKa + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]). A buffer resists pH change; it works best when [A⁻] ≈ [HA], so pH ≈ pKa.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a beaker with acetic acid (HA) and acetate (A⁻). One arrow from added H⁺ to A⁻, one from added OH⁻ to HA.

cards.front: Match each acid with its conjugate base.
cards.back: HCl → Cl⁻, H₂O → OH⁻, NH₄⁺ → NH₃, H₂SO₄ → HSO₄⁻.

cards.front: Order 0.1 M solutions from HIGHEST pH to LOWEST.
cards.back: NaOH → NH₃ → NaCl → CH₃COOH → HCl

cards.front: Name the three kinds of solution in the picture.
cards.back: Unsaturated, Saturated, Supersaturated

cards.front: Ksp of AgCl = [{{Ag⁺}}][{{Cl⁻}}]. For CaF₂: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]{{²}}.
cards.back: Solids are left out of the Ksp expression.

cards.front: Compare Q with Ksp: what does each case mean?
cards.back: Q < Ksp: unsaturated, more can dissolve. Q = Ksp: saturated (equilibrium). Q > Ksp: a precipitate forms.

cards.front: Name the main solubility rules.
cards.back: Always soluble: Group 1 and NH₄⁺ salts, nitrates, acetates. Halides soluble except Ag⁺, Pb²⁺. Sulfates soluble except Ba²⁺, Pb²⁺. Carbonates, hydroxides, sulfides, phosphates mostly insoluble.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a table with 'always soluble' on top and 'insoluble' below it, and place an example salt in each row.

cards.front: What is the common-ion effect?
cards.back: Adding an ion that is already in the equilibrium lowers the solubility of a salt. AgCl dissolves less in NaCl solution than in pure water.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a beaker with AgCl solid and a few ions. Then draw a second beaker with extra Cl⁻ and even less dissolved.

cards.front: Match each salt with its solubility in water.
cards.back: NaNO₃ soluble, AgCl insoluble, BaSO₄ insoluble, (NH₄)₂CO₃ soluble.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two beakers: one clear with dissolved ions, one with white solid at the bottom. Put each salt under the correct beaker.

cards.front: For AB₂ (like CaF₂) with molar solubility s: Ksp = s × (2s)² = {{4s³}}. For AB: Ksp = {{s²}}.
cards.back: Count ions: each formula unit gives 1 Ca²⁺ and 2 F⁻.
cards.sketch_prompt: Write CaF₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻ and under it s and 2s. Multiply the two concentration terms.

cards.front: What is the labeled point on the titration curve?
cards.back: Equivalence point

cards.front: At equivalence, mol H⁺ = mol {{OH⁻}}: Mₐ Vₐ nₐ = {{M_b V_b n_b}}.
cards.back: n = H⁺ or OH⁻ per formula unit; H₂SO₄ has n = 2.

cards.front: What is the pH at equivalence for strong/strong, weak acid/strong base, strong acid/weak base?
cards.back: Strong/strong: 7. Weak acid + strong base: above 7 (the conjugate base is basic). Strong acid + weak base: below 7.

cards.front: Match each indicator with its color change.
cards.back: Methyl orange 3.1-4.4, methyl red 4.4-6.2, bromothymol blue 6.0-7.6, phenolphthalein 8.2-10.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a pH ruler from 0 to 14 and color a bar under it for each indicator's range.

cards.front: How do you pick an indicator?
cards.back: Choose one whose color-change range lies on the steep (vertical) part of the curve around the equivalence point pH.
cards.sketch_prompt: Sketch a titration curve and shade a horizontal band across the steep rise. Write 'indicator range must fall here'.

cards.front: Where is the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration, and what is the pH there?
cards.back: At half the equivalence volume [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa. It is the middle of the buffer region.

cards.front: Put the steps of a titration in order.
cards.back: Rinse burette → fill and read it → add indicator to flask → titrate to a faint lasting color → read the end volume
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a burette over a flask with a swirling arrow. Number the five steps beside it.
items: Fill the burette and read the start volume
Titrate to a faint lasting color change

cards.front: Which ion gives each of the six flame colors?
cards.back: Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cu²⁺, Ba²⁺

cards.front: Match each ion with its flame color.
cards.back: Li⁺ crimson, Na⁺ intense yellow, K⁺ lilac, Cu²⁺ blue-green.

cards.front: How do you test for chloride, bromide and iodide?
cards.back: Add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃. Cl⁻: white precipitate. Br⁻: cream. I⁻: yellow. AgCl dissolves in dilute NH₃.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three test tubes with a white, a cream and a yellow cloud and label each with its ion.

cards.front: How do you test for sulfate?
cards.back: Add dilute HCl, then BaCl₂. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ confirms sulfate. The acid first removes carbonate.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a test tube with a white solid at the bottom and write Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ next to it.

cards.front: How do you test for carbonate and for ammonium?
cards.back: Carbonate: add acid; CO₂ gas turns limewater milky. Ammonium: add NaOH and warm; NH₃ gas turns damp red litmus blue.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a flask with bubbles leading through a tube into limewater turning cloudy. Beside it draw damp litmus turning blue over a warm flask.

cards.front: What do cations give with NaOH solution?
cards.back: Cu²⁺: pale blue precipitate. Fe²⁺: green. Fe³⁺: red-brown. Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺: white, dissolving in excess NaOH. Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺: white, insoluble in excess.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a row of test tubes with colored precipitates (blue, green, red-brown, white) and label the ion above each.

cards.front: Why do metals give flame colors?
cards.back: Heat lifts electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back they emit light of specific colors, and that color is a fingerprint of the metal.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw energy levels with an arrow up (heat) and a wavy arrow down labeled 'light of one color'.

cards.front: Name the five labels on the phase diagram.
cards.back: Solid, Liquid, Gas, Triple point, Critical point

cards.front: Ideal gas law: PV = {{nRT}}. T must be in {{kelvin}}. R = {{0.0821}} L·atm/(mol·K).
cards.back: At STP (0 °C, 1 atm) one mole of gas is 22.4 L.

cards.front: How does N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic) respond to more pressure, more heat and a catalyst?
cards.back: More pressure: shifts right (fewer gas moles). More heat: shifts left (toward the endothermic side). Catalyst: no shift, just faster.

cards.front: Kc = [products]^coefficients ÷ [reactants]^coefficients; pure {{solids}} and {{liquids}} are left out.
cards.back: Example: for 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄, Kc = [N₂O₄] ÷ [NO₂]².

cards.front: ΔG° = {{-RT ln K}}. If K > 1, ΔG° is {{negative}}.
Write the colligative formulas for freezing point and boiling point.
cards.back: ΔTf = i·Kf·m and ΔTb = i·Kb·m. For water Kf = 1.86 and Kb = 0.512 °C·kg/mol. i = particles per formula unit (NaCl ≈ 2).

cards.front: How are Kp and Kc related?
cards.back: Kp = Kc (RT)^Δn, where Δn = gas moles of products minus gas moles of reactants.

cards.front: Why does the solid-liquid line of water slope to the left?
cards.back: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so pressure favors the liquid and the melting point falls as pressure rises.

cards.front: First law: ΔU = {{q}} + {{w}}, where w is work done ON the system.
cards.back: A system that does work loses energy.

cards.front: Heat: q = {{m c ΔT}}. For water, c = 4.18 J/(g·°C).
cards.back: q in joules when m is in grams.

cards.front: ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔHf°({{products}}) - Σ ΔHf°({{reactants}}). ΔHf° of an element in its standard state is {{0}}.
cards.back: Example: ΔHf°(O₂) = 0.

cards.front: Bond enthalpies: ΔH°rxn = Σ bonds {{broken}} - Σ bonds {{formed}}.
cards.back: Breaking bonds costs energy; forming bonds releases energy.

cards.front: Name the two levels in the enthalpy diagram.
cards.back: Reactants, Products

cards.front: State Hess's law and how to handle a reversed or multiplied step.
cards.back: The total ΔH is the sum of the ΔH of the steps. Reverse a step: flip the sign. Multiply a step: multiply its ΔH.

cards.front: When is a reaction spontaneous? (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS)
cards.back: When ΔG < 0. ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0: always. ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0: never. Otherwise it depends on T.

cards.front: Order by increasing entropy.
cards.back: Ice → liquid water → steam
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three boxes with a few particles in a neat lattice, a loose crowd, and spread far apart.

cards.front: What are ΔHfus and ΔHvap for water, and what happens to the temperature during a phase change?
cards.back: ΔHfus = 6.01 kJ/mol; ΔHvap = 40.7 kJ/mol. During a phase change the temperature stays constant while q = n·ΔH.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a heating curve for water with two flat steps (melting at 0 °C, boiling at 100 °C) and label them.

cards.front: What makes lattice energy larger?
cards.back: Higher ion charges and smaller ions. MgO (2+/2-) has a much larger lattice energy than NaCl (1+/1-).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two crystals: Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ close together and Na⁺ with Cl⁻ farther apart. Write 'stronger attraction' on the first.

cards.front: Name the three family endings in the picture.
cards.back: alkane -ane, alkene -ene, alkyne -yne

cards.front: Order the carbon-chain prefixes from 1 to 6 carbons.
cards.back: meth → eth → prop → but → pent → hex

cards.front: What are the three steps of IUPAC naming?
cards.back: 1) Find the longest chain. 2) Number from the end nearest the double bond or first branch. 3) Name branches alphabetically with their numbers, such as 2-methylbutane.

cards.front: What is the difference between constitutional isomers and stereoisomers?
cards.back: Constitutional isomers have the same formula but different connections (butane and 2-methylpropane). Stereoisomers have the same connections but a different 3D arrangement.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw butane as a straight chain and 2-methylpropane with a branch. Under them write C₄H₁₀ for both.

cards.front: What makes a carbon chiral, and what are enantiomers?
cards.back: A chiral carbon has four DIFFERENT groups. Its two mirror images (enantiomers) cannot be stacked on each other and rotate polarized light in opposite directions.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a carbon with four different colored balls and its mirror image next to it. Show that you cannot rotate one into the other.

cards.front: Which butane conformation is the most stable, and which is the least?
cards.back: Anti (CH₃ groups 180° apart) is the most stable. Fully eclipsed (CH₃ groups 0° apart) is the least stable. Gauche (60°) is in between.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three Newman projections of butane (anti, gauche, eclipsed) and rank them with an energy arrow.

cards.front: What do curved arrows show in an arrow-pushing mechanism?
cards.back: They show the movement of an electron PAIR, from the electron-rich place (a lone pair or a bond) to the electron-poor place.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw OH⁻ attacking a carbon with a curved arrow starting at the lone pair and ending at the carbon.

cards.front: Name the two labeled species in the SN2 picture.
cards.back: Nucleophile, Leaving group

cards.front: Summarize SN2.
cards.back: One step; the nucleophile attacks from the BACK, so the carbon is inverted. Rate = k[RX][Nu]. Best on methyl and primary carbons.

cards.front: Summarize SN1.
cards.back: Two steps: the leaving group leaves first, giving a carbocation. Rate = k[RX]. Best on tertiary carbons. The product is a racemic mixture.

cards.front: What is Markovnikov's rule for adding HBr to an alkene?
cards.back: H adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens; Br ends up on the more substituted carbon (the more stable carbocation).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw propene. Add HBr with two arrows: the double bond attacks H, then Br⁻ attacks the secondary carbon. Name the product 2-bromopropane.

cards.front: What happens in an E2 elimination?
cards.back: A strong base removes an H while the leaving group leaves, in one step, making a C=C. Zaitsev: the more substituted alkene is the major product. Heat favors elimination.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a C-C with H on one carbon and Br on the other, opposite each other (anti). Show the base pulling H and a new double bond forming.

cards.front: Order carbocations from LEAST to MOST stable.
cards.back: Methyl → primary → secondary → tertiary
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four carbocations with 0, 1, 2 and 3 alkyl groups and an arrow labeled 'more stable'.

cards.front: Match each reaction with its key feature.
cards.back: SN2 inversion, SN1 carbocation, E2 strong base, addition Markovnikov.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four boxes with a small energy diagram in each: one hump for SN2 and E2, two humps for SN1.

cards.front: Name the six functional groups in the picture.
cards.back: Alcohol, Aldehyde, Ketone, Carboxylic acid, Ester, Amine

cards.front: Match each group with its general formula.
cards.back: R-OH, R-CHO, R-CO-R, R-COOH, R-COO-R, R-NH₂.

cards.front: Order from STRONGEST acid to WEAKEST.
cards.back: Carboxylic acid → phenol → water → alcohol

cards.front: Why is an amine basic?
cards.back: The lone pair on nitrogen can pick up H⁺: R-NH₂ + H⁺ → R-NH₃⁺.

cards.front: How does bromine water tell an alkene from an alkane?
cards.back: Alkenes and alkynes decolorize orange bromine water at once (addition across C=C). Alkanes do not react in the dark.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two test tubes with orange liquid. Show one turning colorless after adding an alkene and the other staying orange with an alkane.

cards.front: How do you tell an aldehyde from a ketone?
cards.back: An aldehyde has an H on the carbonyl carbon and is easily oxidized to a carboxylic acid. Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes only.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a test tube with a shiny silver coating labeled 'aldehyde' and a clear tube labeled 'ketone'.

cards.front: Rank the boiling points of molecules of similar mass by functional group.
cards.back: Alkane < ketone or ether < alcohol < carboxylic acid. More hydrogen bonding means a higher boiling point.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a bar chart with five bars of growing height labeled alkane, ether, ketone, alcohol, carboxylic acid.

cards.front: How do alkanes react?
cards.back: Alkanes are fairly unreactive. They burn (combustion) and react with Cl₂ or Br₂ in UV light by radical substitution.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw methane next to Cl₂ with a UV bulb above. Show CH₃Cl and HCl as products.

cards.front: Name the four pieces of glassware.
cards.back: Graduated cylinder, Burette, Volumetric flask, Erlenmeyer flask

cards.front: Which glassware gives the most precise volume?
cards.back: Volumetric flask and volumetric pipette: one exact volume. Burette: precise variable volume. Beakers and Erlenmeyer flasks are only rough guides.

cards.front: How do you dilute a concentrated acid safely?
cards.back: Always add the ACID to the WATER, slowly, while stirring, with goggles on. Adding water to acid can spatter.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a beaker of water with a small stream of acid going in and goggles beside it. Cross out the reverse.

cards.front: How do you read a meniscus correctly?
cards.back: Put your eye level with the liquid and read the bottom of the curve. Looking from above or below gives a parallax error.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a burette with a curved liquid surface. Mark the correct eye level with a horizontal arrow and wrong angles with crossed arrows.

cards.front: What is the difference between systematic and random error, and between accuracy and precision?
cards.back: Systematic error pushes every reading the same way (fix by calibrating). Random error scatters readings (reduce by repeating). Accuracy = close to the true value. Precision = close together.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four dartboards: accurate and precise, precise only, accurate only, neither.

cards.front: Percent error = |experimental - accepted| ÷ {{accepted}} × {{100}} %.
cards.back: Always divide by the accepted (true) value.
cards.sketch_prompt: Write the formula and fill in a worked example with 2.85 and 2.70.

cards.front: Put the steps of making a standard solution in order.
cards.back: Weigh → dissolve → transfer and rinse → fill to the mark → invert to mix
items: Dissolve it in a beaker with a little water
Transfer to the volumetric flask and rinse
